title: We Put Our Names to It

hero.credit: William J. Stone, engraving of the Declaration of Independence, 1823. National Archives. Public domain.

objective: Children will learn that long ago, in 1776, leaders from 13 places wrote a big paper, the **Declaration of Independence**, and signed their names at the bottom to show they meant it. They will find the biggest signature, count the 13 stars of the first flag, and make and sign a promise of their own.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: When we put our name to something, we are saying: I mean it.

items.text: say that long ago, leaders signed their names on the Declaration to make a promise
items.question: say why the leaders signed their names?
items.screen: say why the leaders signed their names

items.text: find the biggest signature on the Declaration: John Hancock’s
items.question: find the biggest signature?

items.text: count the 13 stars of the first flag, one for each of the first 13 states

materials: The *Show your class* page (page 3), projected or printed
A large sheet of paper with the class promise written at the top
Crayons, including blue and red, and the differentiated handouts
questions: Where do you write your name? Why?
What did the leaders promise? Why did they sign their names?
Which name is the biggest? Can you find a small one?
What promise can our class make, and keep?
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** in *Put Your Name to It*, choose *Our Class Declaration*, fill in your teacher and grade, and let everyone sign. Print it for the wall. Nothing you sign is saved or sent. In *Add a Star*, count the flag’s first 13 stars together.

steps.title: Where do you write your name?
script: Ask: *“Where do you write your name?”* Children may say on a picture, on a card, on their cubby. Ask why. Help them say it: *“Your name says: this is mine. This is me.”* Let each child write their name in the air with one finger.

screen.question: Where do you write your name? Why do you write it there?

steps.purpose: Start from what children know: a name says this is mine, or this is me.
students: Show me with your finger how you write your name.

steps.title: A big paper
script: Show the painting on page 3. *“Long ago, in 1776, leaders from 13 places met in a big room. Those 13 places are now 13 of our states. They wrote a big paper called the **Declaration of Independence**. It said: the king far away should not rule us any more. We will be a new country.”* Children find the man in the red chair: John Hancock, the leader of the meeting. Five men are bringing him the paper.

img.credit: John Trumbull, *Declaration of Independence*, 1818. U.S. Capitol. Public domain.

screen.alt: John Trumbull’s Declaration of Independence: in a high-ceilinged hall hung with red curtains and captured flags, five men stand at the center presenting the draft to John Hancock, seated at the right, while the delegates of the Congress look on

steps.purpose: Meet the leaders, and the big paper they wrote.
students: Find the man in the red chair.
Find the paper on the table.

steps.title: A promise
script: *“At the end of the paper, the leaders made a promise to each other. Then 56 men signed their names at the bottom. Signing your name means: I mean it.”* Add one surprise: George Washington, the most famous of them all, did not sign. He was not even in the room. He was away, leading the army.

screen.text:
They made a promise to each other.
Then they signed their names.

steps.purpose: Hear what a signature means: I mean it.
students: Say it with me: I mean it!

steps.title: The biggest name
script: Show the names at the bottom of the Declaration (page 3). Ask: *“Which name is the biggest?”* Let children point. It is **John Hancock’s**, the man in the red chair, the biggest of them all. Then point to some small ones. *“Big or small, every name says the same thing: I mean it.”*

img.credit: William J. Stone, engraving of the Declaration of Independence, 1823. National Archives. Public domain.

screen.alt: William J. Stone’s engraving of the Declaration: the whole text in a flowing hand, and below it the signatures, every one clear and dark, John Hancock’s largest
screen.caption: The names at the bottom of the Declaration. One is the biggest of all.

steps.purpose: Find the biggest signature, by looking.

steps.title: Your handout
script: Before handing out the pages, say: *“There were 13 states. The first flag had a star for each one: 13 stars.”* Count to 13 together on your fingers and toes. Each child then works on a handout. All three find the biggest name, count 13 stars and end with a signature.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Picture-led. Circle the biggest of three names, color the 13 numbered stars, then write a name or make a mark under a short promise.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Circle the biggest name, count the stars and circle 13, tick the class promises and sign under them, then draw keeping one.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Find the biggest name among them all, draw 13 stars on the flag, then finish *I will…* and sign it.

steps.purpose: Find, count and sign on paper, at the right level for each child.

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the questions on the screen. For each one, the children show a thumb up, sideways or down: *“Can you now say why the leaders signed their names? Can you find the biggest signature? Can you count the 13 stars? Can you make a promise and sign it?”*

screen.hint: Show me: thumb up, sideways or down.

steps.purpose: Check what each student can now do against the objectives.
students: say why the leaders signed their names?
make a promise and sign it?

steps.title: Our class promise
script: Say: *“The leaders made a promise and signed it. Let’s make a promise for our class.”* Read the promise slowly, and let children say it back. The words are from *Our Class Declaration*, in the exhibition’s *Put Your Name to It* room: *“That we will be kind — to our classmates, to our school, and to everyone we meet.”* Put a big sheet with the promise by the door, and let every child sign it during the day, with a name or a mark.

screen.text:
We will be kind —
to our classmates, to our school,
and to everyone we meet.

steps.purpose: Make a promise together, and sign it, as the leaders did.
students: Sign it with your name or your mark.
